a: broke away from the holy land
p: Alexandrinus says Jason "broke away"; Venetus says he "was sent away."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("revolted") and the Vulgate (recessit) agree
readings.en: broke away
readings.plain: broke away from the holy land

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: was sent away
readings.plain: was sent away from the holy land

why: Jason left in revolt (4:26; 5:5–10), not by banishment, so "broke away" fits the story. Venetus's reading is one or two letters longer and probably a copying slip.

p: Swete prints "we brought out the lamps." Venetus, the KJV and the Vulgate have "lit."

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete)
readings.en: we brought out the lamps

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: he brought out

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus (the digital apparatus misprints it εξηφαμεν); Rahlfs prints this reading, and the KJV ("lighted the lamps") and the Vulgate (accendimus lucernas) have it too
readings.en: we lit

why: Swete corrects Alexandrinus's singular to the plural that fits the other verbs. "We lit" is the text of Rahlfs's edition and of most modern versions, and 1 Maccabees 4:50 says the lamps were lit. The Plain keeps Swete's base text, which is the harder reading: a copyist could more easily change "brought out" to "lit" than the reverse. The sense is much the same: the lamps were in use again.

p: Alexandrinus has "year 88"; Venetus adds "hundred," giving 188 (124 BC), as the KJV and the Vulgate do.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("the hundred fourscore and eighth year") and the Vulgate (Anno centesimo octogesimo octavo) agree
readings.orig: ογδοηκοστου και ογδοου] pr εκατοστου και V
readings.en: in the year one hundred and eighty-eight

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: in the year eighty-eight

why: Year 88 of the Seleucid era (224 BC) is long before the events, so the hundred must have dropped out. The Plain departs from Swete's text here and follows Venetus.

p: Swete ends the first letter with "at Jerusalem." Venetus starts the second letter with "those in Jerusalem and those in Judea."

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete), with Swete's punctuation
readings.orig: ἐν Ἰεροσολύμοις. Καὶ οἱ ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ
readings.en: in Jerusalem. And those in Judea

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which puts a stop after the date and adds "those"; the KJV ("the people that were at Jerusalem and in Judea") and the Vulgate (populus qui est Jerosolymis et in Judaea) read the same way. Rahlfs also has "those in Jerusalem," but ends 1:9 with the date
readings.orig: distinx post ογδ. V | εν Ιεροσολυμ.] pr οι V
readings.en: in the year 188. Those in Jerusalem and those in Judea
readings.plain: Those in Jerusalem and those in Judea

why: A Greek letter of this kind ended with its date and place, and the first letter has no date otherwise, so most editors since Bickerman attach the date to it. Rahlfs too ends the first letter with the date. Venetus's added "those" makes the date head the second letter instead. See the note.

t: Did they cut off the heads?
p: Venetus, the KJV and the Vulgate say the priests cut off the heads before they threw them out.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete)
readings.en: throwing the heads out

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("smote off their heads") and the Vulgate (capitibus amputatis) agree
readings.en: taking off the heads, throwing them out
readings.plain: cut off the heads and threw them out

why: Venetus spells out what the shorter text implies, since the men had been cut limb from limb. The sense is the same.

a: the feast of the fire, when Nehemiah offered sacrifices after he had built the temple and the altar
t: "The fire, when" or "the fire that was given"
p: The KJV and the Vulgate say the fire "was given" when Nehemiah offered sacrifice. One later manuscript says Nehemiah "managed" the temple instead of "built" it.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete)
readings.en: and of the fire, when ... having built
readings.plain: the feast of the fire, when Nehemiah offered sacrifices after he had built the temple and the altar

readings.w: The KJV ("and of the fire, which was given us when Neemias offered sacrifice"), following the Vulgate (et diem ignis, qui datus est quando Nehemias)
readings.en: and the day of the fire, which was given when Nehemiah
readings.plain: the feast of the fire that was given when Nehemiah offered sacrifices after he had built the temple and the altar

readings.w: Codex 125, a later minuscule, as reported by Florentine Bechtel (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910); not checked here against the Göttingen apparatus
readings.en: having managed
readings.plain: the feast of the fire, when Nehemiah offered sacrifices after he had managed the temple and the altar

why: No Greek witness in Swete's apparatus has "was given." The Latin fills out a compressed Greek phrase, and the KJV follows it. The sense is close. "Managed" (oikonomēsas for oikodomēsas, one letter apart) looks like a copyist's correction that removes the clash with Ezra 3–6, where Zerubbabel and Jeshua build the temple; the Plain keeps "built", the reading of the main witnesses. See the book page on Nehemiah and the Temple.

p: Venetus repeats "Lord," as the KJV does: "O Lord, Lord God."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the Vulgate (Domine Deus) agrees
readings.en: Lord God

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("O Lord, Lord God") agrees
readings.en: Lord, Lord God

why: The doubled address is common in prayers (Deuteronomy 3:24 in Greek has it), and either could be original. The meaning does not change.

a: he gave a share of them to these men
p: Alexandrinus says the king shared the revenues with the priests; Venetus says he showed favor. The KJV mixes the two.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ οἷς ὁ βασιλεὺς πολλὰ διάφορα ἐλάμβανεν, καὶ μετεδίδου
readings.en: and to whom the king took many revenues, and he shared them
readings.plain: he gave a share of them to these men

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: and the king showed favor and received many revenues and shared them
readings.plain: The king showed favor, received large revenues, and shared them

readings.w: The KJV
readings.en: the king took many gifts, and bestowed thereof on those whom he would gratify
readings.plain: The king took many gifts and gave some of them to those he wished to favor

readings.w: The Vulgate
readings.en: he gave the priests many goods
readings.plain: He gave the priests many good things

why: Alexandrinus's "to whom" is awkward but makes sense with 1:34: the king rewarded the priests who kept the place. The Vulgate, which has the king reward the priests, supports that sense. Venetus smooths the grammar; the KJV seems to join both readings.

p: Alexandrinus has the same name twice; Venetus and Rahlfs have "Nephthai" the second time, and the KJV and the Vulgate "Nephi."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καλεῖται δὲ παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς Νεφθάρ
readings.en: it is called by most people Nephthar

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which also has "the others" for "most people"
readings.orig: πολλοις] λοιποις V | Νεφθαρ 2°] Νεφθαι V
readings.en: the others call it Nephthai

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition
readings.en: it is called by most people Nephthai

readings.w: The KJV ("many men call it Nephi") and the Vulgate (vocatur autem apud plures Nephi)
readings.en: it is called by many Nephi

why: The sentence must contrast two names, so the second name probably differed, as Rahlfs prints it. The Plain keeps Swete's text and marks the problem here and in the note.

a: to finish it and paint it
p: Venetus speaks of the encaustic painter, who burned wax colors into the wall.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("set it out, and paint it") agrees
readings.en: to renew and to paint
readings.plain: to finish it and paint it

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: to burn in (colors) and to paint
readings.plain: to do the encaustic work and paint it

why: Either reading fits the comparison: the abridger is the decorator, not the builder. Venetus gives a more exact craft term.

p: The Greek says Benjamin. Some Latin and Armenian copies, as reported by Bullard and Hatton, say Bilgah, a priestly family.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, as printed by Swete; the KJV and the Vulgate (de tribu Benjamin) agree
readings.en: from the tribe of Benjamin

readings.w: Some Old Latin and Armenian manuscripts, as reported by Bullard and Hatton (not checked here)
readings.en: of Bilgah
readings.plain: from the priestly family of Bilgah

why: Every Greek witness in Swete has Benjamin, and an overseer of the temple need not have been a priest. Bilgah may be a learned correction that makes Simon a priest. Bullard and Hatton, who report it, themselves read "Benjamin" as the priestly family of Miniamin (Nehemiah 12:17, 41). See the note.

a: over the running of the city market
p: The Greek speaks of the market office. The KJV has "disorder in the city," and the Vulgate a wicked plan.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete); Alexandrinus leaves out "over" and spells the word αγορανομειας
readings.orig: περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν πόλιν ἀγορανομίας
readings.en: about the market-office in the city
readings.plain: over the running of the city market

readings.w: The KJV
readings.en: about disorder in the city

readings.w: The Vulgate
readings.en: (the high priest opposing him) to contrive something wicked in the city
readings.plain: because the high priest stood in the way of his wicked plans for the city

why: Agoranomia was the office over the market, a known Greek institution. The KJV and the Vulgate seem not to have understood the word.

p: The father's name differs in every witness.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: Apollonius of Thrasaeus

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, first hand and corrector; Hort conjectured Tharseas
readings.orig: Θαρσιου V* vid Θαρσεου Vᵃ (Θαρσεα coniec Hort)
readings.en: Apollonius of Tharsius / Tharseus

readings.w: The Vulgate (Tharsaeae filium); the KJV has "the son of Thraseas"
readings.en: son of Tharseas

why: The man is not otherwise certain, so the name cannot be checked. The Plain keeps Swete's spelling.

a: because the place was about to be treated with contempt
t: "About to be" or "so as not to be"
p: Alexandrinus has a "not" that is hard to construe. Venetus, Rahlfs, the KJV and the Vulgate lack it, and the Plain follows them.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; Rahlfs, the KJV ("because the place was like to come into contempt") and the Vulgate (pro eo quod in contemptum locus esset venturus) agree
readings.en: because the place was about to come into contempt
readings.plain: because the place was about to be treated with contempt

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: διὰ τὸ μὴ μέλλειν εἰς καταφρόνησιν ἔρχεσθαι τὸν τόπον
readings.en: because of (the wish that) the place not be about to come into contempt
readings.plain: so that the place might not be treated with contempt

why: With the article and infinitive, διὰ τὸ means "because," and "because the place was not about to be treated with contempt" makes no sense. Alexandrinus's "not" can only be forced into a purpose clause. Editors drop it, and the Plain departs from Swete's text here and follows Venetus.

p: The Vulgate and the Douay have the young women run to Onias, not to the gateways.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete); the KJV ("to the gates") agrees
readings.orig: αἱ γυναῖκες σάκκους κατὰ τὰς ὁδοὺς ἐπλήθυνον· αἱ δὲ κατάκλειστοι τῶν παρθένων, αἱ μὲν συνέτρεχον ἐπὶ τοὺς πυλῶνας
readings.en: some ran together to the gateways

readings.w: The Vulgate (procurrebant ad Oniam); the Douay has "some to Onias"
readings.en: ran out to Onias

why: No Greek witness in Swete names Onias here. The Latin may reflect a copy that read a name instead of the word for gateways.

a: the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority
t: Sovereign of spirits, or the spirit of God
p: Venetus has another title; the Vulgate says "the spirit of the almighty God" made the appearance.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("the Lord of spirits, and the Prince of all power") agrees
readings.orig: ὁ τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης ἐξουσίας δυνάστης
readings.en: the Sovereign of the spirits and of all authority
readings.plain: the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the abbreviation πρων usually stands for πατέρων, "fathers"
readings.orig: ο των πνευμ.] ο δε παντων πρων V
readings.en: and the Sovereign of all the fathers
readings.plain: the Sovereign of all the fathers and of all authority

readings.w: The Vulgate (Sed spiritus omnipotentis Dei); the Douay has "the spirit of the Almighty God"
readings.en: but the spirit of the almighty God
readings.plain: the spirit of the almighty God

why: Alexandrinus's title fits the angels who now act. The Latin turns the title into a subject, "the spirit of God."

p: Alexandrinus says the young men were beautiful "in tongue"; Venetus has "in glory," with the KJV and the Vulgate.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (optimi gloria) agrees, and the KJV ("excellent in beauty") has this sense
readings.en: most beautiful in glory

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: most beautiful in tongue

why: The young men have not yet spoken, and the list is of how they looked: strength, glory, clothing. The Plain departs from Swete's text here and follows Venetus.

a: He had become completely helpless, and he had plainly come to know the sovereign power
t: Who came to know God's power?
p: In Swete's Greek, Heliodorus comes to know the power. In Rahlfs and the KJV the bearers do, and the KJV adds "weapons."

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete)
readings.orig: ἀβοήθητον αὐτὸν τοῖς ὅλοις καθεστῶτα, φανερῶς τὴν δυναστίαν ἐπεγνωκότα
readings.en: helpless in every way, having plainly come to know the sovereignty
readings.plain: He had become completely helpless, and he had plainly come to know the sovereign power

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which has "himself" for "in every way" and adds "of God"
readings.orig: αυτον τοις ολοις (χολ. A)] εαυτω V | δυναστιαν (-τειαν Vᵃ) pr του θεου V
readings.en: unable to help himself, having come to know the sovereignty of God
readings.plain: He could not help himself, and he had plainly come to know the sovereign power of God

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition, with ἐπεγνωκότες, nominative plural
readings.orig: ἀβοήθητον ἑαυτῷ καθεστῶτα φανερῶς τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ δυναστείαν ἐπεγνωκότες
readings.en: helpless to aid himself; they had plainly come to know the sovereignty of God
readings.plain: He could not help himself, and they plainly acknowledged God's sovereign power

readings.w: The KJV; its "weapons" matches τῶν ὅπλων in Hanhart's Göttingen text, as reported by Bullard and Hatton, and its "they acknowledged" matches Rahlfs
readings.en: being unable to help himself with his weapons: and manifestly they acknowledged the power of God
readings.plain: He could not help himself with his weapons, and they plainly acknowledged the power of God

why: In Swete's text the participle agrees with "him," so it is Heliodorus who learns, the enemy confessing God's power as he will again at 3:35–39. Rahlfs makes the bearers the subject. The KJV translated a Greek text with both "weapons" and the plural, the printed Greek of its day. Swete's apparatus gives Alexandrinus's word for "in every way" as "χολ.", which the digital text may have garbled (perhaps for ὅπλ., "weapons"); this could not be checked against Swete's page. The Plain keeps Swete's base text.

p: Alexandrinus writes the short form for "Christ" where the sense needs "Lord."

readings.w: Codex Venetus and Swete's text; the KJV and the Vulgate (omnipotente Domino) agree
readings.en: the Almighty Lord

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: the Almighty Christ

why: A Christian scribe's slip between two abbreviated sacred names. See the note.

p: The KJV's sentence lacks "asked," so the king seems to be called Heliodorus.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Alexandrinus, A, 400s AD, as corrected by Swete); the Vulgate (interrogasset) agrees
readings.orig: Τοῦ δὲ βασιλέως ἐπερωτήσαντος τὸν Ἡλιόδωρον
readings.en: when the king asked Heliodorus

readings.w: The KJV
readings.en: And when the king Heliodorus, who might be a fit man

why: The KJV has dropped a word ("asked") in printing or translation. No Greek witness lacks the verb.
